newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's Reinsurance eyes 15 pct premium growth.
newsitem.headline: Australia's Reinsurance eyes 15 pct premium growth.

text.p: Reinsurance Australia Corp Ltd said on Monday it was targeting gross underwritten premium growth of 15 percent in the 1997 calendar year.

Asked if the company was continuing its propectus target growth of gross undwritten premium of 15 percent, Reinsurance managing director Michael Kelly said: "It's what we're aiming at, but it depends on the market."
Earlier, Reinsurance said it had gross written premiums written to date of about A$325 million, compared to about A$300 million at the same time in 1996.
Gross written premium in calendar 1996 was A$527.3 million.
Reinsurance said the year had started well despite a continuing softening in premium rates.

"We think we're a little bit immune to some of those large reductions (in premium rates). We lead a significant percentage of the business that we write -- that business that we don't like we do come off," Kelly said.

Kelly said the company's diverse portfolio allowed it to avoid pockets of the world like Australia and Latin America where premium rates had fallen because of the lack of recent catastrophes in those regions.

Kelly said Reinsurance was starting to see growth in business from its European base office in Nice and was expecting to expand its profile in Latin America and Caribbean growth markets with the opening of an underwriting office in Miami.
Reinsurance was aiming to be amongst the top 10 reinsurers in the world in terms of size and estimated it was now within the top 50, Kelly said.

"We don't write casualty business. The majority of the people in the top 20 write a large share of casualty business. So it is quite an achievement for us to get into that top 20 and not write the largest part of the premium," Kelly said.
About 50 percent of Reinsurance's underwritten business covers property with marine, space and aviation and professional indemnity making up most of the rest of the areas covered.
Reinsurance chairman Peter Cadwallader said the company's own reinsurance cover was substantial in 1996 and Reinsurance would retain that cover this year.
"We spend roughly 13 to 14 percent of every dollar we get on retrocession. We have a very substantial cover and that reduces the risk profile of our whole business," Cadwallader said.
Cadwallader said the company would look at growing through an acquisition if it could be certain it was not inheriting a long term problem or a can of worms that was not evident.
"It would have to have a book we like and people we like," he said.

Kelly said that with the exception of Japan, the Asian reinsurance market was still very immature and although it had tremendous potential, the company's medium term growth would come from other areas.
Kelly said the emerging markets were Korea and Indonesia.
